scopeReview: SPS-2.A.1: intentions and effects of pronatalist, antinatalist and immigration policies. All scenarios hypothetical; no legal advice or claims of current national policy. Consent/instrument distinctions, cohort lags, age composition and spatial implementation are explicit.
varietyReview: Classification table, observational comparison line chart, access map, admissions chart and signed accounting. Other applied tasks distinguish intent/effect, voluntary versus quota instruments, momentum, lag, local planning and timing versus completed family size. All five skills and varied keys/difficulty.
repetitionReview: Prior demographic accounting is now applied to policy components; no existing item is reused. The two evaluation tasks differ: background trends confound causal attribution, whereas cohort histories address tempo versus lifetime totals. No numerical-only duplicate.
referenceNote: Curriculum scope and policy/agency context checked from primary institutions. Original hypothetical scenarios and arithmetic; no copied questions, survey statistics or third-party catalog additions. Automated review is not independent human review.

questions.correctOption: A seeks fewer births, B seeks more births, and C changes immigration admissions.
questions.independentReview: Read the explicit stated goals rather than inferring policy intention from an assumed effect: A fewer unintended births; B more births; C worker entries. Kept migration policy distinct from natality policy.

questions.correctOption: The shared decline means P’s change alone does not establish a causal effect of the package.
questions.independentReview: Computed P change−0.6 and Q−0.7; endpoint difference+0.1. Did not equate difference-in-changes with a proven causal effect absent comparable trends/assignment. The supported inference is a limit on attribution.

questions.correctOption: A uniform national rule can coexist with unequal local access to participating services.
questions.independentReview: Compared district access percentages80/70/30/20 while holding eligibility rules fixed. No household denominator or fertility outcomes are supplied, so neither absolute coverage counts nor causal birth changes follow.

questions.correctOption: Plan B admits 90% of entrants at ages 15–64, compared with 80% under A.
questions.independentReview: Summed A100+800+100=1000 and B100+1800+100=2000; recomputed working-age shares.8/.9. The correct comparison concerns admissions age composition only, not realized employment.

questions.correctOption: It is pronatalist in intent, but the eventual fertility response must be evaluated.
questions.independentReview: Used the explicit objective as the classification criterion. Checked that supporting employment is compatible with a pronatalist aim and that neither legal eligibility nor an incentive guarantees individual fertility changes.

questions.correctOption: A service offering confidential counseling and freely chosen contraception without birth penalties.
questions.independentReview: Compared actual instruments, not merely fewer-birth intentions: A–C impose enforcement/permission constraints; D explicitly preserves voluntary decisions without penalties. Avoided treating antinatalist as synonymous with coercive.

questions.correctOption: Population momentum can sustain many births as large young cohorts enter childbearing ages.
questions.independentReview: Kept fertility per woman distinct from the number of women/cohort size. The specified positive natural change is compatible with lower fertility and a youthful structure; no invented migration balance or immediate stationarity is required.

questions.correctOption: Any additional births must age before entering adult working ages.
questions.independentReview: Applied the fixed passage of cohorts through ages: new births cannot change current adult cohort counts. Distinguished a possible long-run labor-supply contribution from a guaranteed immediate policy effect.

questions.correctOption: An increase of 4,000, because net immigration more than offsets natural decrease.
questions.independentReview: Independently calculated30000−36000+10000=4000. Signed components checked separately; no assumption that the immigration program raises births or determines employment.

questions.correctOption: Use settlement patterns to assess housing, transport and service demand in the receiving cities.
questions.independentReview: Tracked the mismatch between national admission counts and concentrated urban settlement. Local demand assessment follows the supplied spatial distribution; no blanket claim about migrants’ needs or effects on every neighborhood is made.

questions.correctOption: The same cohorts’ childbearing histories over a longer period.
questions.independentReview: Distinguished period birth counts from cumulative cohort fertility. Longer cohort histories address tempo versus completed family size; this is not the same as the separate observational control-trend question and does not by itself identify causation.
